title: Prism Foundry & Fluxlings: two free AI-assisted puzzle prototypes, and what broke when we packaged them
author: GoldtusksStudio
selftext:
We just put two early puzzle prototypes from GoldTusks Studios on itch.io. Both are free to play in the browser, with desktop ZIPs too. We are looking for feedback on the core mechanics before expanding them into larger games.



Prism Foundry: fire tiles into descending fragments and complete hollow rectangular boundaries to clear them.

[https://goldtusksstudio.itch.io/prism-foundry](https://goldtusksstudio.itch.io/prism-foundry)



Fluxlings: move colorful creatures around a gravity chamber, connect matching pieces, and trigger chain reactions.

[https://goldtusksstudio.itch.io/fluxlings](https://goldtusksstudio.itch.io/fluxlings)



AI was used during development for code, graphics, and text. The recent release work used Codex to export the Expo web builds, prepare Electron desktop packages, fix integration problems, and check the games in the browser and on macOS. The itch pages include the AI disclosures.



One concrete snag: a web build loading locally did not mean the packaged app would render correctly. Pixi shader generation hit the Electron shell's content security policy, so we switched to its static shader helpers while keeping the policy in place. The browser exports also needed asset paths that worked under itch.io's nested hosting URLs. Windows and Linux packages are cross-built and still need native testing; all desktop downloads are unsigned.



That is the part I would like to discuss here: AI helped get the builds together, but exporting, checking actual rendering, and validating the first few interactions still needed separate attention. What checks do you use to decide an AI-assisted prototype is ready for people outside your development setup?



If you try either game, I would especially appreciate feedback on where the tutorial becomes unclear, whether the controls feel natural, and whether the central mechanic makes you want another round.
